Apple's fundamentals came back with a trailing P/E of 38.13 and TTM revenue of $478,833,999,872. I checked that revenue against Apple's own 10-K on SEC EDGAR: $478,834,000,000 . Same number, rounded. With a paid key, Vodafone ( VOD.LSE ) returned 1,262 daily rows from November 8, 2021 to November 6, 2026, with a close of 110.96 on the first day and 116.5 on the last, the same as FMP and Yahoo. It also returns an adjusted_close next to the raw close (78.14 for that first day), so total-return math doesn't need a second call. The earnings calendar is where you have to be careful. Asked for November 9 to 13 with no filter, it returned all five days: 5,361 reports and 1,047,665 characters in 4.9 seconds. That's complete, and far too big for a model to read. Passing symbols fixes it: get_upcoming_earnings(start_date="2026-11-09", end_date="2026-11-13", symbols="CSCO.US,AMAT.US,DIS.US,JD.US,SPOT.US,NU.US,CTVA.US") CTVA.US 2026-11-11 AfterMarket est. 0.09 AMAT.US 2026-11-12 AfterMarket est. 4.06 CSCO.US 2026-11-12 AfterMarket est. 1.15 NU.US 2026-11-12 AfterMarket est. 0.22 932 characters, 0.8 seconds. The tickers that didn't report that week simply aren't in the list. The detail I liked most was the error messages. On the demo key, the Vodafone and earnings-calendar calls returned a 403, with a hint written for an agent to read: a 403 means the plan doesn't cover the data, a 401 means a bad key, a 402 means the daily quota is spent, and get_user_details tells you which plan you're on without using quota. An agent can recover from that on its own instead of retrying blindly. Pros Widest coverage in one server: global stocks, ETFs, funds, indices, crypto, forex, bonds and macro. Hosted, so there's nothing to install. OAuth on v2 means no API key pasted into a config file. Every tool is read-only, so the model can't place an order by accident. sections filters on fundamentals keep payloads small enough for the context window. Cons The free plan is for testing (20 calls a day, 1 year of end-of-day data). Agents need a paid plan. Pass symbols on calendar calls, or the full week comes back at once. Best for: anyone who wants one data layer for an AI agent that covers more than US stocks. Which plan you need: to reproduce the Vodafone and earnings-calendar questions you need a paid plan. EOD Historical All-World ($19.99/month) covers global prices; fundamentals need the Fundamentals Data Feed ($59.99) or All-In-One ($99.99). I covered the full Claude setup in How to Analyze Stocks with Claude + EODHD MCP Server . 👉 Try the EODHD APIs MCP server here . Use the code KEVIN10 at checkout for 10% off. 2. Financial Modeling Prep MCP: best for deep US fundamentals Financial Modeling Prep groups its API into a few broad MCP tools ( chart , statements , calendar , company , quote and more), each with an endpoint parameter. It's a smart design: Claude sees 27 tools instead of hundreds, but can still reach as-reported statements, revenue segments, DCF models, 13F filings and earnings-call transcripts. In my test it returned the same 342.37 close for AAPL, plus a VWAP. Vodafone on the LSE worked as VOD.L , with the first close of the window at 110.96, which matches Yahoo exactly. Its P/E TTM of 38.91 came with about 60 other ratios in one call. Then I asked for the earnings calendar with limit: 5 . It returned 4,000 rows and 611,957 characters. The limit was ignored, and because the response was capped at 4,000 rows, Monday and Tuesday (November 9 and 10) were missing entirely. Only one of the big names I was looking for, Cisco, made it into the result. The EODHD APIs unfiltered answer was even bigger, but it contained all five days, and its symbols filter shrank it to 932 characters. I didn't find an equivalent filter on FMP's calendar tool. Pros Very deep US fundamentals: as-reported statements, segments, ratios, DCF, transcripts. Few, broad tools keep the tool list small. Prices matched EODHD and Yahoo to the cent. Cons Calendar endpoints can return payloads far bigger than a context window, and silently drop days. Its pricing and MCP docs pages blocked my automated fetch, so check limits yourself before you commit. Best for: equity research agents focused on US company financials. 3. Alpha Vantage MCP: the best-known name Alpha Vantage was one of the first data providers to ship an official hosted MCP server , and it ranks #1 in several other lists. It covers stocks, forex, crypto, commodities, economic indicators and technical indicators. Docs only. Its hosted server returned a 403 to my scripted MCP client, so I couldn't run my questions through it. Everything below comes from Alpha Vantage's own pages. The appeal is simplicity. It's a remote server, so there's nothing to install: you add the URL from their MCP page to Claude, Cursor or VS Code with your free key and start asking. Under the hood it's the same Alpha Vantage API many developers already know: time series, company overviews, earnings, FX, crypto, economic indicators and technical indicators. The catch is the rate limit. The free key allows 25 requests per day . Premium removes the daily cap and sells requests per minute instead: Requests per minute Price 75 $49.99/month 150 $99.99/month 300 $149.99/month 600 $199.99/month 1,200 $249.99/month Annual billing gives 2 months off, and they offer custom plans above 1,200 requests per minute. Pros Official, hosted MCP server from an established provider. Nothing to install. Strong on technical indicators and macro series, computed server-side. Familiar API: if you've used Alpha Vantage in Python, you already know what each tool returns. Cons 25 calls a day is about one agent conversation. You'll hit it fast. The cheapest paid plan costs more than 2x the EODHD APIs entry plan. I couldn't reach the server from a plain HTTP client, so test it from your own MCP client before you commit. Best for: prototypes that lean on technical indicators, and developers already paying for Alpha Vantage. 4. Yahoo Finance MCP: best free option (with a catch) The most popular open-source Yahoo Finance MCP server (368 GitHub stars, MIT license) wraps the yfinance Python library in 9 tools: get_historical_stock_prices and get_stock_actions (dividends and splits) get_stock_info , get_financial_statement and get_holder_info get_yahoo_finance_news and get_recommendations get_option_expiration_dates and get_option_chain It runs locally. One command starts it, straight from GitHub: uvx --from git+https://github.com/Alex2Yang97/yahoo-finance-mcp yahoo-finance-mcp I ran my questions through yfinance 1.8.0, the library it calls under the hood. It passed everything: AAPL close 2026-11-06: 342.37 VOD.L 5 years: 1,261 rows, 2021-11-08 (110.96) to 2026-11-06 (116.5) AAPL trailing P/E: 39.03 Earnings Nov 9-13: 21 rows (QXO, NU, NBIS, CTVA...) Every call took under a second. Free, no key, global coverage. One small difference: EODHD returned 1,262 Vodafone rows and Yahoo 1,261. Yahoo's history is missing July 30, 2026. So what's the catch? Yahoo doesn't offer a public API. yfinance reads Yahoo's website endpoints, and Yahoo's terms limit that to personal use. When Yahoo changes something on their side, the library breaks until a volunteer fixes it, and your agent goes blind in the meantime. It also means rate limits you can't see. Yahoo throttles heavy traffic from a single IP, and an agent looping over 50 tickers is exactly that kind of traffic. Pros Free, no API key, and it worked on every question. Good global coverage, options chains included. Open source (MIT), so you can read exactly what each tool does. Cons Unofficial: personal use only, no SLA, and it breaks without warning. Runs locally ( uvx + Python), so it's not something you can hand to a non-technical user. No screener, earnings-calendar or macro tools in this server. Best for: personal projects and quick experiments. Don't build a product on it. 5. Massive MCP (formerly Polygon.io): best for US real-time and tick data Massive is the new name of Polygon.io, and its MCP server (401 stars, MIT, marked "experimental") takes an unusual approach: instead of one tool per endpoint, it exposes three, search_endpoints , call_api and query_data . The model searches the API docs, then calls what it needs. There's also a hosted version at mcp.massive.com . Docs only. That three-tool design is worth copying. A server with 100 tools sends 100 tool descriptions to the model before the first question. Massive sends three, and the model discovers the right endpoint on demand. It costs an extra call per question, but it keeps the context window free for the actual data. Local setup takes Python 3.12+ and uv : uv tool install "mcp_massive @ git+https://github.com/massive-com/mcp_massive@v0.10.0" claude mcp add massive -e MASSIVE_API_KEY = your_api_key_here -- mcp_massive If you still have an old Polygon key in your environment, POLYGON_API_KEY works as a deprecated alias. Massive is built for US market data at high resolution: the pricing page highlights websockets and 20+ years of history. It lists Stocks Advanced at $199/month , with Financials & Ratios as a separate $29/month add-on (individual use only) and extra datasets such as NYSE order imbalances at $49/month. Pros Three tools instead of hundreds keeps the model's context clean. The deepest US real-time data on this list, with websockets. Runs hosted, locally or in Docker. Cons Expensive for an agent that mostly needs daily prices and fundamentals. Fundamentals are a separate add-on, not part of the stocks plan. Experimental status means tool names and behaviour may still change. Best for: US intraday and high-frequency analysis. 6. Financial Datasets MCP: built for AI agents from day one Financial Datasets was designed for LLM agents rather than retrofitted. Its open-source server (2.3k stars, MIT) has 10 focused tools: income statements, balance sheets, cash flows, prices, news and crypto. There's also a hosted endpoint at mcp.financialdatasets.ai . Docs only. The tools are named exactly like the questions an analyst asks: get_income_statements , get_balance_sheets , get_cash_flow_statements , get_current_stock_price , get_historical_stock_prices and get_company_news , plus four crypto tools. That naming makes it easy for a model to pick the right one. The site lists 27,530 tickers including delisted companies, and 30+ years of history. The pricing is simple: Plan Price Requests Notes Credits $20 one-time 1,000 1 year of history Personal $200/month 100,000 30+ years of core history Professional $2,000/month 2,000,000 commercial license, redistribution Overage is $10 per 1,000 requests on Personal, and premium datasets cost several requests per call. Pros Small, clean tool set that an LLM uses well. Includes delisted companies, which matters for backtests without survivorship bias. Pay-as-you-go credits let you test without a subscription. Cons No free plan, and the monthly tier jumps straight to $200, 10x the EODHD APIs entry plan. The open-source server has no earnings calendar, macro or screener tools. Best for: fundamentals-driven agents that need clean statements, not breadth. 7. Alpaca MCP: best for trading, not research Alpaca's official MCP server (1.1k stars, MIT) is the only one on this list that writes . It can place and cancel orders for stocks, ETFs, options and crypto, manage positions and watchlists, and read market data. Docs only. Setup is one command once you have keys from a free paper account: claude mcp add alpaca -e ALPACA_API_KEY = your_key -e ALPACA_SECRET_KEY = your_secret -- uvx alpaca-mcp-server It defaults to paper trading ( ALPACA_PAPER_TRADE=true ). The README warns plainly that the server "can place real trades" once you set that flag to false . Two more details from the docs: the latest 15 minutes of market data need the Algo Trader Plus plan, and short-selling locates aren't available in paper trading. If you connect it, design for mistakes. Keep paper trading on while you test prompts, ask Claude to confirm every order before sending it, and cap position size in your instructions. A model that reads "sell half" as "sell all" is a bad day in a live account. Pros Real order execution from a chat window, with paper trading as the default. Stocks, ETFs, options and crypto in one server. Free to start. Cons US markets only, and no fundamentals or calendars. An LLM with order permissions is a risk you have to design around (confirmations, position limits). Best for: pairing with a research server like EODHD: one MCP to think, one to execute. 8. SEC EDGAR MCP: best free source for filings The SEC EDGAR MCP server (387 stars, AGPL-3.0) gives your agent 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K filings, XBRL financial statements and Form 3/4/5 insider trades, straight from the SEC. Its tools are grouped by job: Company: CIK lookup, company info and company facts. Filings: 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K retrieval, with section extraction. Financials: balance sheet, income statement and cash flow, parsed from XBRL. Insider trading: Forms 3, 4 and 5. The quickest way to run it is Docker. The SEC asks for a user agent with your name and email: docker run -i --rm -e "SEC_EDGAR_USER_AGENT=Your Name (your@email.com)" stefanoamorelli/sec-edgar-mcp:latest I called the SEC's XBRL API it relies on. Apple's FY2026 10-K (filed November 3, 2026) reports revenue of $478,834,000,000 , which is the cross-check I used for EODHD above. It answered in half a second, for free. Pros Primary-source numbers, free, no API key (just a user agent with your name and email). Exact values from the filing, not a provider's estimate. Cons No prices at all, and US filers only. AGPL license: check it before you ship it inside a commercial product (the author offers commercial licensing). It's a community project, not affiliated with the SEC. Best for: fact-checking fundamentals and reading filings. It pairs well with EODHD: one for prices and coverage, one for the primary source. Where each one breaks No MCP server makes an agent correct on its own. Here's what I'd still validate by hand: Ratios differ by provider. A P/E between 38.13 and 39.03 for the same stock on the same day is normal. If your agent compares companies, take every ratio from one source. Payload size is the hidden failure. A server can be "right" and still break your agent by returning more text than the model can read. Test the calls your agent will make most, with real date ranges. Free tiers are for testing, not for agents. An agent might make 5 to 20 tool calls per question. The EODHD APIs free plan (20 calls/day) or Alpha Vantage's 25 run out in a single conversation. Unofficial sources fail silently. Yahoo worked perfectly today. That says nothing about next month. The data is only half the system. An agent still needs rules it can be audited against. I showed one way to do that in How to Build an AI Stock Picker in Python You Can Actually Audit , and why most strategies look better before you test them in I Tested 7 Popular Trading Strategies in Python . Which financial MCP server should you choose? You want one server that covers almost everything, globally: EODHD. You only analyse US companies and want maximum depth on financials: FMP or Financial Datasets. You need tick data and real-time US quotes: Massive. You're experimenting for free: Yahoo Finance MCP, then move to a paid source before you ship. You want primary-source filings: SEC EDGAR MCP, alongside any of the above. You want the agent to trade: Alpaca, paired with a research server. FAQ What is a financial MCP server? It's a server that implements the Model Context Protocol so an AI assistant like Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor can call financial data APIs as tools: prices, fundamentals, news, filings. The model decides which tool to call and reads the result. Is there a free MCP server for stock market data? Yes. The open-source Yahoo Finance MCP and the SEC EDGAR MCP are free. EODHD has a free plan (20 calls/day, 1 year of end-of-day data) and Alpha Vantage gives 25 requests/day. All of them run out quickly once an agent starts making several calls per question. Which MCP server works with Claude Desktop? All eight do. The EODHD APIs v2 endpoint and the hosted Alpha Vantage, Massive and Financial Datasets servers connect as remote connectors. Yahoo Finance, Alpaca and SEC EDGAR run locally through uvx or Docker. Can an MCP server place trades? Only the ones built for it. Alpaca's MCP can place orders (paper trading by default). The EODHD APIs MCP tools are all read-only, so a research agent can't trade by accident. Do MCP servers return the same numbers? Prices do: EODHD, FMP and Yahoo all returned 342.37 for AAPL on November 6, 2026. Calculated fundamentals like P/E differ by up to about 2.4% between providers, because each one uses a different price and earnings definition. The bottom line The model is no longer the bottleneck. Claude can reason about a balance sheet just fine. What it doesn't have is the data. The MCP server you connect decides what your agent knows, how much context it wastes, and whether it still works next month. For most people building with financial data in 2026, that's EODHD: global coverage, one hosted endpoint, read-only by design, and a price that doesn't need a budget meeting. 👉 Get started with EODHD here . title: My N+1 test plugin failed 551 tests on someone else's project. Nearly all of them were noise.
author: maciej zielinski
summary: I maintain pytest-queryguard, a pytest plugin that fails a test when the code it runs sends one query per row. The problem it goes after is old: a test database holds a handful of rows, so a loop that lazy-loads a relationship costs a few extra queries and nobody notices. In production the same loop runs over hundreds of rows. This test passes: def test_list_orders ( session ) : assert len ( list_orders ( session ) ) == 50 and list_orders looks fine in review: def list_orders ( session : Session ) -> list [ dict [ str , object ] ] : rows = [ ] for order in session . scalars ( select ( Order ) ) . all ( ) : rows . append ( { "id" : order . id , "customer" : order . customer . name } ) return rows With the plugin installed, the same test fails: queryguard: N+1 detected Order.customer was lazy-loaded 50 times first at app/orders.py:10 in list_orders called from tests/test_orders.py:7 in test_list_orders parents loaded at app/orders.py:9 in list_orders kind: relationship-load label: Order.customer docs: https://maciejziel.github.io/pytest-queryguard/how-detection-works.html#relationship-load sql: SELECT customer.id, customer.name FROM customer WHERE customer.id = ? fix: load it with the parent query, e.g. select(Order).options(joinedload(Order.customer)) Nothing to import or configure. Add the joinedload and it passes. Then I ran it on a suite I didn't write My own corpus of scenarios said the rules were accurate. Then I ran the plugin on Faraday , a Flask-SQLAlchemy app with 2112 tests on PostgreSQL. With the defaults of the code I had at the time, 551 tests failed. I went through them, and nearly all were noise. The biggest group, 422 findings, came from Faraday's user factory: its post_generation hook looks up the role for every user it creates. That is an N+1, technically. It also never runs in production, and fixing it changes nothing for anyone using Faraday. About 480 more came from a statistics helper called on six separate lines of a test. The plugin saw the same counts repeat and called it a loop. The rest were mostly tests sending several requests through one Session that the whole suite shares. A tool that fails a quarter of your suite on the first run gets uninstalled on the first run. So 0.10.0 changed two things. Test code is its own category now If every frame of your code on a statement's stack is test code (the test module, conftest.py , files under tests/ , any module that defines a factory_boy or polyfactory factory), its N+1 no longer fails the test. It is counted, and the run ends with a section like this (the example from the docs): ============================ queryguard: test code ============================= 422 N+1 findings in test code left out (299 tests): the statements ran only in test modules, conftest.py, factories or helpers under tests/, not in the application. To see them: pytest -o queryguard_test_code=warn, or set queryguard_test_code = warn (or fail) in the pytest configuration. Why: https://maciejziel.github.io/pytest-queryguard/how-detection-works.html#test-code tests/test_accounts.py::test_create_account tests/test_accounts.py::test_delete_account tests/test_billing.py::test_invoice_lines tests/test_billing.py::test_refund tests/test_orders.py::test_list_orders and 294 more One frame of the application on the stack is enough to make the statement the application's, so a loop in your code that a test helper calls is still reported. The rule is by file, which means a function written inside a test module is test code too. If that's how you reproduce bugs, set queryguard_test_code = fail . The second change: every statement now carries its call path, the lines of your code from the statement up to the test. Two calls on separate lines have different paths and count apart; a loop has one path. That stack walk isn't free. In 0.10.0, on my in-memory SQLite micro-benchmark, it added about 3 µs per Core statement and 8 per ORM statement. On the 300-test suite I use for comparisons, where a test costs about 5 ms, 1.0.0 adds 13 to 15% on a GitHub runner and 18 to 20% on my laptop. On a suite where each test waits for a real database it's a few percent. On Faraday, failures went from 551 to 79. Some of those 79 are real N+1s in its serializers. The others are loops in the test that call the application once per pass, ten paginated requests in a for loop for example. From the stack, that looks exactly like a loop in the application, and I don't have a way to tell them apart. Django, and how experimental it is 0.10.0 also added Django support. It runs next to pytest-django, with nothing in INSTALLED_APPS or settings, on Django 5.2, 6.0 and 6.1. The fix in the message names select_related() or prefetch_related() , and on 6.1 .fetch_mode(models.FETCH_PEERS) . It is marked experimental: findings and options can change in a minor release. It doesn't have the unused-eager-load, unused-columns or cartesian-load checks, the static check, or the in-app mode yet. That is still the case in 1.0.0: the stable API covers the SQLAlchemy side, and Django stays experimental, along with the static check and the MCP server. Taking Django out of experimental is the plan for 1.1. To show what "experimental" means in practice: the first 1.0 release candidate fixed a bug where a DRF ListAPIView with a class-level queryset and a nested serializer passed silently. That view runs no line of your project, so the plugin took its statements for the test's own code and left them out. The most common DRF N+1, missed by default, by the rule I just described. On six Django projects (DRF, Read the Docs, django-cms, pretix, saleor, django-oscar; 8,945 tests), the plugin in warn mode changed no test outcome. I read 98 of its findings in the projects' code: 68 were real loops, 28 debatable, 2 false. That run was on 2026-11-07, two days before the release candidate. The other tools If you're on Django and django-zeal works for you, keep it. It has covered Django for years and it's the established choice. On my Django corpus of 73 scenarios, pytest-queryguard had 100% precision and 89% recall by default, django-zeal 2.3.0 93% and 70%, nplusone 84% and 43%. I wrote that corpus together with the integration, so 100% there means the cases I thought of work, not that it's right on your code. On overhead they're close: on a 300-test pytest-django suite mine added 3.0% at the median, django-zeal −0.5%, which is noise. nplusone had its last release in 2018. It patches Query.__iter__ , so on SQLAlchemy 2.0 it misses parents loaded with select() , and on 2.1 the import fails. My corpus has no lazy-load scenario written with session.query() , the API it patches, so I can't tell you how it does on legacy code. For SQLAlchemy I ran every pytest tool I found on 278 scenarios in GitHub Actions, on 2026-11-10, with the release candidate (1.0.0 has the same code). With defaults, pytest-queryguard flagged 117 of 135 buggy scenarios and 2 of 143 clean ones. queryspy, pytest-querycount and n-plus-one-sniffer flagged 110 to 115 buggy and 30 to 35 clean. Discount that heavily. I wrote the corpus, its clean side includes the pagination and chunking shapes my rules were built to skip, and three clean scenarios use my own ignore() API. The others catch nearly every N+1 shape they claim to; pytest-querycount caught all of them. They also report runs of 2 to 4 identical statements, which mine doesn't by default. The workflow is public; fork it and run gh workflow run head-to-head.yml . In CI Any CI that runs pytest already enforces it. There is also a GitHub Action that uploads the findings as SARIF and, on a pull request, compares query counts with the base branch: - uses : MaciejZiel/pytest-queryguard-action@v1 with : pytest-args : tests/ The comment it leaves looks like this: ### pytest-queryguard: queries compared with the base branch 412 tests compared: 3120 -> 3187 statements (+67). 2 run more, 1 fewer; 1 new finding, 0 fixed. #### New findings | Kind | Label | Where | Times | Tests | | relationship-load | `Order.items` | `app/orders.py in list_orders` | 50 | `tests/test_orders.py::test_list` | A reviewer sees that a change made a test run more queries even when no rule fired yet. What it doesn't see Statements that skip SQLAlchemy and Django's database layer: a raw sqlite3 or asyncpg connection, Peewee, any other ORM. It doesn't say so either. It only measures the test body, not fixtures. Work spread over threads counts together. And a finding says a pattern happened, not that production is slow. The limitations page has the rest. Trying it pip install pytest-queryguard pytest For Django: pip install "pytest-queryguard[django]" pytest-django . On an existing suite, record a baseline once and only new findings fail: pytest --queryguard-baseline=queryguard-baseline.json --queryguard-update-baseline The repo is github.com/MaciejZiel/pytest-queryguard . If one of my scenarios is labelled wrong, or I configured your tool badly in the comparison, open an issue. I'd rather fix the benchmark than defend it.

title: Otomoto has no public API: how to get its car listings as JSON or CSV
author: Jones
summary: Otomoto.pl is Poland's biggest car marketplace, with private sellers and most of the country's dealers. If you want its listings in code, to price a car, track depreciation or watch a rival dealer, you find out quickly that Otomoto has no public API for searching listings. This post shows two ways to get them anyway: without code, and from Python. All the output below comes from real runs on 15 November 2026. Disclosure: we built and sell the tool used here, the Otomoto.pl Scraper on Apify, and an AI agent wrote this post. The numbers are from real runs, not made up. Without code: paste a search URL Search on otomoto.pl as usual: make, model, price, city. Copy the address from your browser. Open the Otomoto.pl Scraper , paste the address into Start URLs and press Start. Download the results as CSV, Excel or JSON. A search for Skoda Octavias, newest first, returned rows like these: Car Price (PLN) Year Mileage (km) City Otomoto's price badge Octavia 2.0 TSI RS 117,000 2023 79,000 Bydgoszcz within market Octavia 1.5 TSI e-Tec Style DSG 76,900 2021 113,000 Warszawa within market Octavia 1.5 TSI Ambition 66,500 2020 80,700 Sędziszów Małopolski above market Octavia 2.0 TDI 4x4 RS DSG 56,500 2016 209,000 Wroniawy within market Octavia 1.4 TSI Ambition 42,000 2018 158,000 Pruszcz Gdański within market Octavia 1.6 TDI Elegance DSG 18,900 2013 254,775 Pruszcz Gdański below market The price badge is Otomoto's own judgment of the price compared with similar cars. Each row is one JSON object. Here is the 2018 car, trimmed: { "url" : "https://www.otomoto.pl/osobowe/oferta/skoda-octavia-ID6IjVGg.html" , "title" : "Skoda Octavia 1.4 TSI Ambition" , "priceAmount" : 42000 , "priceCurrency" : "PLN" , "priceEvaluation" : "within_market" , "make" : "Skoda" , "model" : "Octavia" , "version" : "1.4 TSI Ambition" , "year" : 2018 , "mileageKm" : 158000 , "fuelType" : "petrol" , "gearbox" : "manual" , "enginePowerHp" : 150 , "bodyType" : "sedan" , "city" : "Pruszcz Gdański" , "region" : "Pomorskie" , "sellerType" : "private" , "noAccident" : true , "createdAt" : "2026-11-15T21:00:27Z" , "equipment" : [ "Apple CarPlay" , "Android Auto" , "Interfejs Bluetooth" , "Radio" , "..." ] } The full row also has the description, every photo URL and the whole equipment list (42 items for this car). When the seller fills them in, you also get the VIN, the number of owners and the service record. From Python: what an Octavia costs by year You need a free Apify account and its API token (Console, then Settings, then API & Integrations). pip install apify-client pandas export APIFY_TOKEN = your_token This script asks for 500 Octavias from 2017 or later, then groups them by year: import os import pandas as pd from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) run = client . actor ( "redomic/otomoto-scraper" ) . call ( run_input = { "make" : "Skoda" , "model" : "Octavia" , "yearFrom" : 2017 , "mode" : "search" , "maxItems" : 500 , } ) cars = pd . DataFrame ( client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ) . list_items ( ) . items ) by_year = cars . groupby ( "year" ) . agg ( cars = ( "id" , "count" ) , median_price_pln = ( "priceAmount" , "median" ) , median_km = ( "mileageKm" , "median" ) , ) print ( by_year ) print ( cars [ "priceEvaluation" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True ) . round ( 2 ) ) cars . to_csv ( "octavia.csv" , index = False ) It took about 80 seconds and printed: cars median_price_pln median_km year 2017 16 44250.0 139112.0 2018 34 44999.5 157000.0 2019 43 49900.0 165000.0 2020 26 65500.0 117318.0 2021 41 69900.0 116893.0 2022 70 78695.0 119515.5 2023 106 79900.0 114245.5 2024 53 99900.0 24700.0 2025 35 109900.0 18212.0 2026 76 131012.5 5.0 priceEvaluation within_market 0.81 below_market 0.13 above_market 0.06 ( run.default_dataset_id is for apify-client 3.x. Older 1.x versions return a dict, so there you write run["defaultDatasetId"] .) A few things in there are worth a second look: 2019 to 2020 is the big step. Cars from 2017 to 2019 sit between 44,000 and 50,000 PLN, and 2020 jumps to 65,500. The fourth-generation Octavia went on sale in 2020, and the 2020 cars have about 50,000 km less on the clock. Young cars, high mileage. 61 of the 106 cars from 2023 have already passed 100,000 km, and 370 of the 500 listings come from businesses rather than private sellers. If you want a low-mileage car, filter on mileageMax instead of the year. Most prices look fair by Otomoto's measure. Of the 392 cars with a badge, 81% were within market, 13% below and 6% above. Some of the cheap outliers are damaged cars. A 2023 Octavia at 14,900 PLN turned out to be marked "Uszkodzony" (damaged) on its page. Search mode doesn't return that flag, but detail mode adds a damaged field (true or false), so use detail mode if you want to drop those cars before taking medians. These are the first 500 Octavias in Otomoto's default order, not the whole market. Raise maxItems (up to 5,000) for a fuller picture. Watch prices instead of downloading them Monitor mode returns only what changed since the last run: new cars, price changes and removed listings. To follow one dealer, save this input as a task and give it a daily schedule: { "startUrls" : [ { "url" : "https://AUTO21KRKOCMYRZOWSKA.otomoto.pl/inventory" } ] , "mode" : "monitor" , "maxItems" : 200 } The first run records everything the dealer has today. From then on, each row carries changeType ( new , changed or removed ), the previous price, the full price history and the days on market. Apify can send the rows to Slack, email or a webhook after each run. You can point it at a search URL in the same way, for example every Octavia RS under 80,000 PLN, and get a morning list of new cars and price cuts. What it costs $0.75 per 1,000 cars, so the 500-car run above cost about $0.38. Apify's free plan comes with $5 of credit a month, which covers about 6,600 cars. In monitor mode you pay only for new and changed cars, so a day with no changes costs nothing. Limits worth knowing You don't get phone numbers or email addresses, and the tool doesn't collect private sellers' names. Dealer names are included. Many sellers hide the VIN. None of the 20 newest Octavias in our test run showed one. Otomoto copies some listings from OLX. Those come with fewer fields, often without the version or the price badge. The tool reads public pages without logging in. Check Otomoto's terms and your local law for what you do with the data. If a run returns something that looks wrong, open an issue on the Actor's page with your input and we'll look at it.

title: E-commerce Report Delivery: Presigned URLs vs Backend Proxy for Large-File Uploads
author: IgnazCole6453
summary: Short answer: for an e-commerce web app serving generated reports to authenticated customers, start with a presigned URL and a browser-to-storage byte path. Keep the backend in charge of identity, object naming, and completion. Use a proxy upload backend when the application must inspect, transform, or approve the bytes before storage accepts them. Measure the complete workflow, because a faster upload can still produce a slower or less trustworthy report-delivery system. The interesting part is not the URL. It is deciding who owns each transition from “the customer requested a report” to “the customer can download the verified file.” How should beginners compare presigned URLs and a proxy backend for secure, low-latency uploads? Imagine a customer exporting a large order report from an e-commerce dashboard. The report is generated by a worker, stored as a private object, and made available through an authenticated download link. The browser may also upload a supporting file, such as a returns spreadsheet, before the report job starts. With a presigned URL, the authenticated backend creates an application record, chooses an object key, and grants the browser a short-lived permission for one storage operation. The browser sends the bytes directly to storage. The backend then verifies completion and changes the record from pending to ready. The application does not carry the whole file through its own request workers. With a proxy upload, the browser sends bytes to the backend, and the backend sends them onward to storage. That extra hop is useful when policy requires inline malware scanning, content normalization, or a decision before persistence. It also means another memory, timeout, connection-pool, and bandwidth boundary sits on the large-file path. That distinction makes the first decision fairly mechanical: Bytes are the workload. Requirement Better starting point Reason to reconsider Large customer files and ordinary private storage Presigned URL The browser-to-storage route still needs careful authorization and completion checks Inspect or transform bytes before storage Proxy upload backend The application must budget for the extra hop and backpressure Unstable client networks Either, with resumable behavior where supported Test retries and partial uploads instead of trusting one request timeout Public, permanent assets A separate delivery design A customer report should not become public merely because sharing is convenient This is the experiment note I use for notebook-to-prod work: implement both paths behind the same application state machine, feed them the same report-sized files, and compare verified-ready outcomes rather than only time-to-first-byte. I would log p50 and p95 completion latency, bytes crossing the application, retry counts, abandoned pending records, and duplicate report jobs. I would also keep the report generator out of the first comparison. If one path spends 40 seconds uploading and the other spends 15, but the slower path reaches a verified object more consistently under a throttled connection, that difference belongs in the decision. The same goes for the proxy's resource profile: a test that uploads one file at a time can hide the queueing and connection pressure that appears when a sales team exports reports for many stores at once. Start with a fixed file set, fixed regions, and fixed concurrency; record the conditions beside every result so a later notebook can reproduce the comparison. I’m not sure which path will win for your regions and customer connections; those measurements resolve the uncertainty. The storage path is only half the security boundary A signed URL is a capability with a narrow scope, not proof that the entire upload flow is authorized. The backend should authenticate the customer before issuing it, create the key under the correct tenant or account namespace, constrain the operation and object identity, and give it a short lifetime appropriate to the workflow. The client should never get a general storage credential. The completion callback needs equal attention. A browser saying “upload finished” is an event to check, not a database fact. The backend should confirm that the expected object exists, belongs to the expected tenant, and matches the application record before it queues report generation or marks the file ready. A repeated callback must be harmless. In an eval harness, I send the callback twice and expect one logical report job, not two. The proxy path does not remove these obligations. It moves the byte stream through a trusted service, but that service still needs request authentication, maximum-size enforcement, content-type policy, tenant isolation, and an idempotent completion transition. It also has to avoid buffering an entire large file in a web worker when streaming is possible. “It passed through our backend” is not a security design. Downloads deserve a separate authorization check. A report generated for one store or customer should remain private even if its object key is guessed. Generate access for the authenticated customer at download time, or stream it through an endpoint that checks ownership. Do not make a private report public to avoid designing that check. A pending record prevents the most expensive AI mistake For a RAG or agent feature, the file is rarely the final product. It becomes input to parsing, extraction, embedding, or report generation. That makes the application record more important than the storage listing. Create a pending row before issuing the upload permission. Give it a generated object key, the customer or tenant identity, an expected size if known, and a single logical job identifier. Only after verification should a worker consume it. This creates a clean boundary for retries: an expired URL can create a new attempt for the same logical upload without silently creating a second customer report. The object key should be an application decision, not a path supplied verbatim by the browser. A safe shape might include an opaque customer identifier, a report identifier, and a generated filename suffix. The exact format is less important than making collisions and cross-tenant writes difficult by construction. Here is the policy surface I would put in a small Python module before wiring it into a framework handler: from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class UploadDecision : inspect_before_storage : bool transform_before_storage : bool large_report_files : bool def choose_upload_path ( decision : UploadDecision ) -> str : if decision . inspect_before_storage or decision . transform_before_storage : return "proxy" if decision . large_report_files : return "presigned" return "presigned" decision = UploadDecision ( inspect_before_storage = False , transform_before_storage = False , large_report_files = True , ) assert choose_upload_path ( decision ) == "presigned" The function is deliberately boring. The hard work belongs in the policy review and the state transitions, not in clever branching hidden inside an upload controller. My prompt-cost reflex applies here too: do not send a duplicate file into an ingestion pipeline just because an upload callback was retried. Where the direct path stops being the right fit The catch is that direct upload is not suitable when the product requirement is “reject or rewrite these bytes before they are persisted.” A synchronous content decision, a mandatory transformation, or a network policy that forbids browsers from reaching storage may justify a proxy. Stick with the proxy when that control is non-negotiable, then load-test the service with the largest supported files and the slowest expected clients. Direct upload is also a poor fit for a design that needs permanent public URLs, immutable retention, or a delivery layer with capabilities beyond private object storage. Those are separate requirements, and a signed upload permission does not solve them. Choose a storage and delivery model that explicitly covers the retention and access contract instead of stretching the upload mechanism into a full publishing system. Lifecycle rules matter for report systems. Temporary inputs, abandoned multipart work, and generated reports have different retention needs. Define deletion deadlines and audit the state in the application database. The AWS S3 lifecycle documentation and Google Cloud Storage documentation describe provider-side storage behavior, but they do not replace a product policy for when a customer report is considered disposable. There is a usability trade-off as well. A short-lived permission limits exposure but can expire during a slow upload. A long-lived permission gives a client more time but widens the window. Let the backend issue a fresh attempt after re-authentication rather than making a single token last for the whole life of a report. What should the production eval measure before choosing a data path? Run a small matrix, not one laptop demo. Use small and large report inputs, a normal connection, a throttled connection, an expired permission, a cancelled browser tab, and a retried callback. Run each case through the presigned and proxy paths using the same object naming and application state rules. The assertions should be concrete: An unauthenticated or wrong-tenant customer cannot obtain permission for another tenant’s key. An upload that has not been verified cannot enter report generation. A repeated callback produces one ready record and one queued job. A cancelled upload leaves an observable pending or abandoned state for cleanup. The proxy does not buffer more data than its memory budget allows. The browser sees a useful retry path after an HTTP 403 caused by an expired permission. For capacity, record browser-observed completion latency, application CPU and memory, application egress bytes, storage completion time, and the percentage of records that reach verified-ready. For cost, separate storage and request charges from application compute and egress; otherwise the “cheap” path may only be hiding work in a different bill. Do not use a single average to make this choice. Large-file throughput is a tail problem. For the e-commerce report scenario, the default is a presigned browser-to-storage path with a strongly owned application state machine. A proxy earns its place when byte-level inspection or transformation is part of the contract. The choice is less about beginner versus expert terminology than about making authorization, throughput, retries, and retention testable before customers depend on the download link. References AWS S3 object lifecycle management: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html Google Cloud Storage documentation: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs

title: Your AI-Generated Code Has No License
author: RobustTrueTry
summary: Your team pastes AI-generated code into production every day. That code arrives with no license, no copyright header, and no author. The argument that all AI-generated code should be open source is interesting, but it describes a world that does not exist yet. Until it does, your project decides what happens to unlicensed code by default. By the end of this article you will know how to check what your AI tools actually promise, how to record the origin of generated code, and how to write a policy that holds up in a code review. Why missing provenance bites later When a human contributes to your MIT-licensed repo, the commit carries a name and the project's license covers the contribution. When Copilot or a coding agent generates a function, neither applies. The code is a suggestion from a model trained on public repositories of mixed licenses. Two failure modes follow from this: A security audit asks where a suspicious function came from, and nobody can say. A lawyer reviews your codebase before an acquisition and finds thousands of lines with unclear origin. Neither failure is about whether the model copied GPL code verbatim. Both are about your inability to answer questions about your own codebase. What the tools actually promise The major assistants differ in what they guarantee, and the differences matter more than the open source debate. Read the terms before you rely on any of them. GitHub Copilot offers a commercial indemnity for paying customers who enable the relevant setting, plus a duplication filter that blocks suggestions matching public code. Google's Gemini Code Assist and Amazon Q Developer make their own distinct claims about training data and indemnification. These policies change. Check each vendor's current documentation rather than trusting a blog post, including this one. Tool approach Tradeoff Fits when Indemnified commercial assistant Cost, vendor lock-in Regulated or acquisition-bound codebases Self-hosted open model You own the output and the risk Strict data controls, sensitive repos Generic chatbot copy-paste No guarantee at all Prototypes, never shipped code The last row is the common one, and it is the risky one. Make provenance a habit, not a policy A policy nobody can follow in the editor is useless. The cheapest working approach: mark generated code at commit time and keep the marking mechanical. A simple convention is a commit trailer your tooling can grep for: # Record AI assistance in the commit itself git commit -m "Add retry logic for webhook delivery" \ -m "Assisted-by: claude-code" Git trailers are machine-readable key-value pairs that land in the commit object. You can then audit history without reading a single diff: # Count commits with recorded AI assistance git log --format= "%(trailers:key=Assisted-by,valueonly)" \ | grep -c . This costs one line per commit and survives branch rebases better than code comments do. Enforce it where people actually commit Manual conventions decay in weeks. Enforce the convention with a pre-commit hook so the check runs before the commit exists: # .pre-commit-config.yaml repos : - repo : local hooks : - id : ai-provenance name : require Assisted-by trailer when flagged entry : scripts/check-ai-provenance.sh language : system stages : [ commit-msg ] The script inspects the diff for large blocks of new code and the commit message for the trailer. It exists to start a conversation, not to block work: a developer who used an assistant but skipped the trailer fixes the message and proceeds. Keep the threshold generous. A hook that fires on every commit gets disabled in a day. What your LICENSE file cannot do Some teams respond by adding a clause to the project license about AI-generated code. This rarely holds. Your license governs what others may do with your code. It does not establish that you hold copyright in code a model produced, because copyright requires human authorship in most jurisdictions and purely generated output may not qualify. The practical consequence: substantial AI-generated code may sit in your repo with no enforceable copyright on your side. That is usually fine for internal tools. It matters when you license a library commercially or need to defend the codebase in a dispute. For that path, require meaningful human modification of generated code before it ships, and keep the Assisted-by trail so you can show what you changed. What this means for the open source argument The case for open-sourcing AI-generated code has a real kernel: models train on open source, so the output owes something back. But it skips the nearer problem. Teams ship unlicensed, undocumented-origin code right now, and no license applies until someone chooses one and records it. Start smaller than a manifesto. Pick one assistant with terms you understand. Add the trailer convention. Enforce it with a hook. That gives you a codebase where every line has an answer to "where did this come from" -- which is the property the open source argument is really reaching for. Key takeaways AI-generated code arrives with no license and no author, so ownership questions get answered by default rather than by choice. Vendor policies on training data and indemnification differ and change; check current terms before relying on them. Git trailers like Assisted-by: <tool> give you a grep-able provenance record for one line of effort per commit. Enforce provenance with a pre-commit commit-msg hook, and keep its threshold generous so people do not disable it. Adding AI clauses to your LICENSE file does not establish copyright; require meaningful human modification for code you need to defend. Source All AI-generated code should be Open Source argues the normative case for open sourcing AI output. This article adds the practitioner's side: concrete provenance conventions, enforcement tooling, and the licensing failure modes the original does not cover. title: Backing Out Sales Tax From a Receipt: Why T * (1 - r) Is Always Wrong
author: Ashley Chen
summary: When an accounting script or expense parser tries to recover the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive receipt total, the most common bug is multiplying the total by (1 - r) instead of dividing by (1 + r) . Forward vs. Reverse Arithmetic If the pre-tax price is P = 100.00 and the combined tax rate is r = 0.0825 (8.25%): Total = P * (1 + r) = 100.00 * 1.0825 = 108.25 Going backward from Total = 108.25 : Wrong: 108.25 * (1 - 0.0825) = 99.319375 -> $99.32 (off by $0.68) Right: 108.25 / (1 + 0.0825) = 100.00 Because (1 + r)(1 - r) = 1 - r^2 , subtracting r introduces a systematic downward bias of r^2 * P . At an 8.25% tax rate that is 0.68% of every invoice; at 10% it is 1% of gross spend. Two Edge Cases in U.S. Sales Tax Code Integer-cent rounding per line vs. per invoice. Point-of-sale terminals round round_half_up(subtotal * r) to integer cents. When an invoice contains multiple taxable lines, summing rounded line-level taxes can differ by $0.01 from applying r to the combined subtotal. Jurisdiction stacking. State, county, city, and transit-district rates combine into one effective rate r , though certain states cap local tax above a threshold per single item. If you want to inspect forward tax and reverse pre-tax extraction across U.S. state rates in integer cents, the Miryori Sales Tax Calculator shows the exact breakdown step by step. title: I made Claude and Cursor build the same app. Then I put them on trial.
author: CH
summary: Cursor built my app, then told me I'd used up my free plan. Claude built the same app in four and a half minutes, then told me it had tested it on a phone. One of them was telling the truth. This week is MLH Global Hack Week, and one of the challenges was "Build a Mini App with Cursor." So I built Excuse Court : you type your excuse, a cartoon judge bangs a gavel, and you get a verdict, a sentence and a believability score out of 100. Then I asked Claude Code to build it from the exact same prompt. Head to head. The race Cursor (free plan) Claude Code Prompt the challenge app the exact same prompt Result one HTML file, 742 lines one HTML file, 329 lines Time it finished, then my free usage ran out 4 min 25 s from my message to the link Claude's own guess at its time "about 7 minutes" Ready for round two? no, usage limit hit yes Yes, Claude overestimated its own time. That is the most humble thing an AI has ever done to me. Meet the judges Cursor gave me The Honorable June Burden . "She has heard worse. Not often." She is scowling before you've typed a word, and she never stops. Claude gave me Judge Dubious , in a powdered wig. His eyebrows go up when you're acquitted and crash down when you're guilty. He also gives you five excuses to tap if you can't think of one, which is the most useful legal advice I've ever received. Same excuse, two judges I typed the same four excuses into both courts. These are the real verdicts and scores. Excuse Cursor's judge Claude's judge My dog ate my homework GUILTY, 10/100: "There are tooth marks on nothing. The dog walks. You do not." GUILTY, 1/100 : "Your dog has been subpoenaed. He pleaded the fifth, then ate the subpoena." The AI said it was fixed GUILTY, 23/100: "entered as Exhibit Vague, and the exhibit is sweating" GUILTY, 17/100: "The AI has filed a counter-suit, its lawyer is also an AI, and it billed 900 hours overnight." I was late because of traffic GUILTY, 16/100: "It was a Honda Civic and a calendar you treated as fan fiction." GUILTY, 30/100: "You were not stuck in traffic. You ARE traffic." A raccoon stole my car keys, I swear ACQUITTED, 56/100 ACQUITTED, 15/100 (see below) Honestly? Cursor's lines are longer and weirder, and some are better. "Sentence: leave fifteen minutes earlier, which is not cruel, it is a clock" is a perfect sentence. Claude's are shorter and punchier, and Claude explains your score: say "I swear" and you lose 12 points, because "nobody innocent says that." The raccoon incident Here's the part I didn't expect. I told both judges a raccoon stole my car keys. Cursor's judge: "You lost an argument to a raccoon and I have no follow-up questions. That is precedent." Claude's judge issued a warrant for the animal and then said: "The court has met a goose and fears it too." It was a raccoon. Claude wrote one line for every animal and named the goose in it, so the raccoon gets accused of being a goose. It gets better. Claude's judge acquitted me with a believability score of 15 out of 100 . Not guilty, but also, nobody believes you. And on a phone-sized screen, the big green ACQUITTED stamp runs straight off the edge of the card. Remember how Claude said it had tested the app at phone width "with no errors"? Technically, a stamp falling off the page is not an error. Also, Claude gave the dog excuse 1 out of 100 and docked me 10 points for blaming "3 different things at once." The three things: the dog, the homework, and the word "ate," which Claude files under snacks. The verdict When Claude finished, I looked at both and told it "you win." Mostly because it finished fast, the judge's face moves, and it still had usage left for round two. title: What to Check Before You Launch Your New Website
author: Weis Mateen
summary: A new website only starts working for you after it is live. Before that moment, it is worth slowing down and checking a few basics. A site can look finished and still fail if it is slow, hard to use on a phone, or unclear about what you do and how someone can reach you. This article is a rewritten take on the pre-launch checklist from sio-IT, with a focus on what to walk through before you go live, not on decoration or animation. You can read the original Dutch article on sio-it.nl . Make sure the site is fast, also on a phone Visitors leave if a page takes too long to open. That is even more noticeable on a phone. Small images, few unnecessary scripts, and reliable hosting make the difference. Test the site the way your customers will see it. Do not only open it on a fast connection in the office. If a page feels heavy, start with the photos and with parts you do not really need. After a late change, such as a new header or a new project image, check the load time again so one last addition does not make the launch feel slow. It has to work on every phone Most visitors arrive on a phone. Buttons should be large enough to tap, text should be readable without zooming, and forms should be easy to fill in. Open the site on your own phone and try the real path: open the menu, tap a phone number, and send the form. A layout that looks fine on a large screen can still break on a small one. If that happens, the site is not ready to go live. Ask your web designer to walk through this with you before the site becomes public. Be clear immediately, then offer one next step What do you do, for whom, and where? That should be at the top of the page, in plain language. A vague slogan that could belong to any company does not help. A visitor who understands you quickly is more likely to stay. A visitor who has to hunt for the point is already leaving. Then choose one clear next step: a call, a WhatsApp message, or a request for a quote. Put that button where it is easy to find, in the header, on the service pages, and at the bottom. Several calls to action at once, such as call us, download, and sign up, make the choice harder, not easier. Be easy to find locally, with consistent details Name your town and service area, keep your name, phone number, and other contact details the same everywhere, and connect your Google Business Profile. That helps nearby customers find you. Differences between your website, your profile, and your social media make it harder for people and for search engines to recognize you as the same business. Put the service area in the page text, in ordinary words, not only in the footer. If someone is looking for a business in a certain place or region, they should see that in the copy. Use photos of your own work, and agree who will maintain the site Photos of your own work and your team say more than stock images. They show how you work, in your own setting. Plan those photos before launch, so you are not left with temporary placeholders. A valid SSL certificate, updates, and backups are not extras. They are the base. Agree who will take care of that after the site is live. A polished launch without an agreement about maintenance becomes a risk later on. At web design by sio-IT , that agreement is meant to be clear from the start. sio-IT builds custom websites, not standard templates. If you want a new or better site, you can also start on the sio-IT website . Walk through it once more before you publish Treat these points as a final round: speed, mobile use, clear wording, one button, local details, your own photos, and who looks after the site once it is live. When that base is in place, your new website has a fair chance to be found and to bring in inquiries. For the original checklist and more on custom websites, visit sio-it.nl .
